comparison-sort-bound.name: Comparison sort lower bound
comparison-sort-bound.oneLiner: The theorem guaranteeing that no comparison-based sorting algorithm can beat O(n log n) in the worst case
comparison-sort-bound.description: The comparison sort lower bound proves that an algorithm sorting purely by comparing elements has to make at least O(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. In the decision tree model, telling apart n! permutations requires a height of at least log2(n!), and by Stirling's approximation that is O(n log n).
comparison-sort-bound.significance: It proves that merge sort, heap sort, and the like are asymptotically optimal, and it pins down exactly where the performance of comparison sorting stops.

n.description: The total count of elements to be sorted.

\\log n.description: The logarithmic part of the comparison count, coming from the height of the decision tree.

n!.description: How many arrangements of n elements are possible. It is the lower bound on the number of leaves in the decision tree.

\\Omega(n \\log n).description: It says the worst-case comparison count is at least proportional to n log n.

realWorldExamples: The theoretical basis for choosing an algorithm when sorting a database index
Analyzing the time complexity of a sorting-based solution in a programming contest
The grounds for the performance guarantees of library sort functions such as Timsort

master-theorem.name: Master theorem
master-theorem.oneLiner: The theorem that sorts divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) into three cases
master-theorem.description: The master theorem is the standard tool for analyzing the recurrences of divide-and-conquer algorithms. Depending on how the number of subproblems a, the size reduction factor b, and the combining cost f(n) relate, it sorts the recurrence into one of three cases and hands you the closed-form time complexity immediately.
master-theorem.discoverer: Jon Bentley, Dorothea Haken, James Saxe
master-theorem.significance: It is the key tool for analyzing divide-and-conquer algorithms, letting you read off the complexity of merge sort, binary search, Strassen's matrix multiplication, and more at a glance.

T(n).description: The running time of the algorithm on an input of size n.

a.description: How many subproblems the recursion splits into. It is an integer of at least 1.

n/b.description: The input size of each subproblem. b is a constant greater than 1.

f(n).description: The non-recursive cost spent on the dividing and combining steps.

\\log_b a.description: The threshold value that, compared against the polynomial degree of f(n), decides which of the three cases applies.

realWorldExamples: Getting O(n log n) out of merge sort's T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)
Getting O(log n) out of binary search's T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)
Analyzing Strassen's matrix multiplication, T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2)

hamming-distance.name: Hamming distance
hamming-distance.oneLiner: The distance measure counting how many corresponding positions differ between two strings of equal length
hamming-distance.description: The Hamming distance is defined as the number of positions at which two binary strings (or general strings) of the same length differ. It is the central concept of error detection and correction coding theory, and it is used directly to measure how many bits got flipped in a data transmission.
hamming-distance.significance: It is the design basis of error-correcting codes (Hamming codes), and it is used widely in communication systems, DNA sequence comparison, and similarity search.

x.description: One of the two strings being compared.

y.description: The other of the two strings being compared.

d(x,y).description: How many corresponding positions differ between x and y.

n.description: The common length of the two strings.

realWorldExamples: Detecting how many bit errors are in received data in network communication
Setting the minimum Hamming distance when designing the error correction capability of a QR code
Measuring the number of DNA mutations as a Hamming distance in bioinformatics

boolean-complement.name: Complement law of Boolean algebra
boolean-complement.oneLiner: The basic law of Boolean algebra that the OR of any logic variable with its complement is always 1 (true)
boolean-complement.description: The complement law says that ORing a variable A with its negation A' always gives 1, and ANDing them always gives 0. It is the most basic rule for simplifying logical expressions, and it is applied constantly in digital circuit design and in programming.
boolean-complement.significance: It is the starting point for optimizing digital logic circuits and simplifying logical expressions, and the foundation of every theorem in Boolean algebra.

A.description: A Boolean variable taking the value true (1) or false (0).

A'.description: The negation of A. It is 0 when A is 1, and 1 when A is 0.

+.description: It denotes the OR operation in Boolean algebra.

1.description: The always-true value. It shows that the result of the OR must be 1.

realWorldExamples: Applying the complement law when minimizing a logical expression with a Karnaugh map
Checking that x | ~x == 1 when optimizing bitwise operations in programming
Removing unnecessary gates in FPGA circuit design

handshaking-lemma.name: Handshaking lemma
handshaking-lemma.oneLiner: The lemma that the degrees of all vertices in a graph add up to twice the number of edges
handshaking-lemma.description: The handshaking lemma follows from the fact that in an undirected graph each edge contributes to the degree of exactly two vertices. So the total of all degrees is always even, and the number of vertices with odd degree must be even too.
handshaking-lemma.significance: It is the most basic theorem of graph theory, underpinning network analysis, tests for Eulerian paths, and graph validity checks.

\\sum \\deg(v).description: The number of incident edges added up over every vertex of the graph.

2|E|.description: The total number of edges multiplied by 2. Since each edge contributes to two vertices, it equals the total degree.

\\deg(v).description: The number of edges incident to the vertex v.

|E|.description: The total count of edges in the graph.

realWorldExamples: Analyzing the relation between the total number of friendships and each person's connection count in a social network
Checking that port counts and link counts agree when validating a computer network topology
Checking the precondition for deciding whether an Eulerian path or circuit exists

password-entropy.name: Password entropy
password-entropy.oneLiner: The formula that measures a password's information content in bits from the alphabet size N and the length L
password-entropy.description: The password entropy formula takes the number of possible combinations when choosing L characters from an alphabet of size N and converts it with a logarithm into an information content in bits. The higher the entropy, the more resistant the password is to brute force attack, which makes it the quantitative basis for security policy.
password-entropy.discoverer: Claude Shannon (the concept of information entropy)
password-entropy.significance: It is the standard measure for objectively gauging password strength in information security, and it gives security policy and authentication system design a quantitative footing.

H.description: The information content in bits. It is the logarithm of the number of attempts a brute force attack needs on average.

N.description: How many distinct characters are available. It is 26 for lowercase only, and over 90 for upper and lower case plus digits and symbols.

L.description: How many characters make up the password.

\\log_2.description: The function that converts a count of possibilities into bits.

N^L.description: How many password combinations are possible in all.

realWorldExamples: Building a password strength meter for a website's sign-up form
Setting a minimum password entropy requirement in a corporate security policy
Comparing the strength of passphrases against random character strings
